analysis.one_liner: Taxes carbon in fuels at $40 per ton and returns the money as $1,000 credits per person.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, vote, or a single cosponsor and died in committee when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would place a fee on the carbon in coal, oil, and natural gas produced or imported into the United States, starting at $40 per ton and rising with inflation. The money would come back to families through a refundable $1,000 tax credit for every taxpayer and every dependent, phased out only for households earning above $157,000 per person. A family of four would collect $4,000 a year, far more than the fee would add to its fuel bills. The bill was referred to the tax-writing committee and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary households collect the credit. Because the fee is charged per ton of carbon, a typical family's extra fuel costs would be well under the $1,000-per-person credit it receives, so most families come out ahead financially while the fee nudges the economy toward cleaner fuels and lowers carbon pollution that drives climate change and air-quality harms.

how_it_helps.text: Every individual taxpayer and every dependent receives a refundable $1,000 credit, so a family of four would get $4,000 a year, paid even to families that owe no income tax.
The credit only begins phasing out above $314,000 of income for couples, meaning the rebate is aimed at ordinary earners rather than the wealthy.
Both the carbon fee and the credit rise with inflation, so the rebate keeps pace with the fee over time.

Charging $40 per ton of carbon gives coal, oil, and gas producers and importers a direct financial reason to reduce emissions, addressing air quality and climate change as described in the bill's subject areas.

analysis.who_pays: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers and importers pay the fee at the mine or well, and they would pass part of it to consumers through higher fuel and electricity prices. Higher-income households also pay in the sense that they receive no credit once their income exceeds the phase-out thresholds.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and large fuel consumers

drawbacks.text: Fuel and electricity prices would rise immediately when the fee takes effect, while the credit arrives at tax time, so households feel the cost months before the rebate — a squeeze that falls hardest on drivers and rural households with tight budgets.
A $40 per ton fee is modest by the standards of most carbon-pricing proposals, so the emissions reduction would be real but limited.

The bill was introduced by one member with no cosponsors and no committee hearing, so it never received the scrutiny of a markup where design problems like the rebate timing could be debated and fixed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is straightforward and progressive: the fee raises fossil fuel prices, the credit returns more money than most families would pay, and the phase-out concentrates the benefit on middle- and lower-income households. The main real cost is timing — consumers pay the fee at the pump and the thermostat before their tax refund arrives — and the bill's biggest weakness was political, not structural: it never got a hearing or debate where that could have been addressed.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee in July 2018, got no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney introduced the bill on July 26, 2018, during the final months of the 115th Congress.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee that handles tax legislation, and that is the last action of any kind in its record.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors, and the committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, so it never reached the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal, oil, and gas producers avoided a $40-per-ton fee on their products, and no member other than the sponsor ever had to take a position on it. Households that would have collected the $1,000-per-person credit are left with neither the rebate nor the emissions reduction.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers; the bill died unexamined

for.name: Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to Ways and Means; it gained no cosponsors during his remaining months in the session.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction; never scheduled a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from referral in July 2018 until the Congress ended in January 2019 without any hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: Kevin Brady
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee of jurisdiction, never scheduled the bill for consideration during its six months of pending status.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so no party split can be measured; the single sponsor was a Democrat and the bill sat in a committee chaired by a Republican with a majority for six months without action.

industries.note: Coal is the most carbon-dense fuel, so a $40 per ton carbon fee would raise coal's effective cost more than any other fuel's, speeding its decline. Its interest in blocking the bill ran against the rebate and cleaner air ordinary households would have gotten.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and importers
industries.note: The fee is charged at every domestic well and on every imported shipment of fuel, directly raising the cost of petroleum and natural gas. Consumers would pay part of this at the pump but get it back through the credit, so the industry's loss is not the public's loss.
